title: Database Control Plane
seoTitle: Design a Control Plane for a Distributed Database
description: Design the control plane for a managed distributed database — cluster provisioning, desired-state reconciliation, failover, scaling, and safe rolling operations.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Database Control Plane?
blocks.text: A distributed database has a **data plane** (the nodes that store and serve data) and a **control plane** (the system that creates clusters, scales them, replaces failed nodes, applies upgrades and backups). Managed services like Amazon RDS, Cassandra operators, or Netflix's internal platforms are control planes.

items: Users should be able to create, resize and delete database clusters via an API.
The control plane should detect failed nodes and replace them automatically.
The control plane should perform rolling operations — version upgrades and config changes — without downtime.
Users should be able to see the status of each cluster and in-progress operations.
Query routing (handled by the data plane).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: A control-plane outage must never take down the data plane — databases keep serving traffic.
Operations must be safe: never remove more replicas than the cluster can tolerate.
Operations are long-running (minutes to hours) and must survive control-plane restarts.
Manage thousands of clusters and tens of thousands of nodes.

lines: - data plane survives control plane outage
blocks.caption: Control Plane Requirements

items: **Cluster spec (desired state)**: engine version, node count, instance type, config.
**Cluster status (observed state)**: nodes, their health, versions, roles.
**Operation**: a long-running workflow (create, scale, upgrade, replace node) with steps and status.

blocks.text: The API writes the **desired state** (spec) to a durable store and returns immediately. It doesn't perform the work inline — a **reconciler** notices that desired and observed state differ and launches an operation to close the gap, like a Kubernetes controller.

An **agent** on every node reports health and database-level status (is it in the ring, is replication caught up). If a node is unhealthy beyond a threshold, the observed state no longer matches the spec, and the reconciler starts a "replace node" operation: provision a new node, join it, stream data, then decommission the old one.
Upgrades proceed **one node (or one rack/zone) at a time**: drain, upgrade, restart, wait until healthy and caught up, then continue. Each step is gated by health checks.
Cluster status and operation progress are read from the state store and surfaced through the API and UI.
1) How do we run long operations reliably?

blocks.title: Run operations inside API request handlers

approach.text: Call cloud APIs and wait for completion during the request.

challenges.text: Operations take hours; any restart loses progress and leaves clusters half-changed.

approach.text: Model each operation as a workflow (Temporal, Step Functions, or a state machine persisted in the database). Every step — provision VM, join node, stream data, verify — is idempotent and its result is recorded, so after a crash the workflow resumes exactly where it left off. Only one operation per cluster runs at a time (a per-cluster lock) to avoid conflicting changes.

challenges.text: Workflow versioning when operation logic changes mid-flight.

blocks.text: 2) How do we make operations safe?

approach.text: Wait for each node to be healthy before moving on.

challenges.text: Doesn't prevent two independent operations (or an auto-replacement during an upgrade) from taking down multiple replicas at once.

approach.text: Before removing or restarting any node, check a **disruption budget**: with replication factor 3 and quorum reads/writes, at most one replica of any token range may be down. Operate by rack/zone so replicas in other zones keep quorum. Automatically pause and alert if error rates or latency regress, and support rollback.

challenges.text: Requires the control plane to understand the database's replica placement, not just VMs.

blocks.text: 3) What if the control plane itself goes down?

The data plane must be fully independent: nodes keep serving, replicating and electing leaders without the control plane. The control plane only changes topology. Run it in multiple zones, keep its state in a replicated store, and ensure reconcilers are **level-triggered** (they compare state rather than relying on missed events), so after an outage they simply catch up.

quiz.question: What is the most important property of the control plane relative to the data plane?
options: Its outage must not take down the databases
quiz.explanation: Databases keep running; the control plane only changes topology.

quiz.question: What does desired-state reconciliation do?
options: Continuously compares spec to observed state and acts to close the gap
quiz.explanation: It's the controller pattern used by Kubernetes operators.

quiz.question: What is a disruption budget?
options: A limit on how many replicas can be unavailable at once
quiz.explanation: It ensures operations never break quorum.

quiz.question: Why model operations as durable workflows?
options: Operations take hours and must resume after control-plane restarts
quiz.explanation: Persisted, idempotent steps make long operations recoverable.
